name: Chloe Harrington
presenting_complaint: Vomiting, abdominal pain and rapid deep breathing over 12 hours

medications: Insulin aspart with meals per carbohydrate counting
medical_history.social: University student. Recent gastroenteritis in household. Admits missing several insulin doses because she 'wasn't eating'.

validation_criteria.presenting_scenario: A 24-year-old woman with type 1 diabetes presents with 12 hours of vomiting, abdominal pain and deep rapid (Kussmaul) breathing. She has missed insulin doses during an intercurrent illness. She is drowsy (GCS 14), tachycardic and mildly hypotensive. Obs: BP 104/62, HR 122, RR 30, SpO2 98% RA, BGL 28.4 mmol/L. She has the smell of ketones on her breath.
validation_criteria.task: Document your assessment and initial management as the admitting RMO.

subjective: Symptom history: polyuria, polydipsia, vomiting, abdominal pain, lethargy; onset over 12 hours
Precipitant screen: missed/reduced insulin during illness, intercurrent infection (gastroenteritis), and explicitly ask about SGLT2 inhibitor use (euglycaemic DKA)
Insulin regimen, adherence and last dose taken; usual glycaemic control
Red-flag/associated symptoms: fever, dysuria, cough, chest pain, focal infection source
Fluid intake/output, oral tolerance and conscious-state trend; document allergies and full medication list
objective: Assess hydration and haemodynamics: mucous membranes, capillary refill, postural BP, HR
Bedside capillary blood ketones (or urine ketones) AND venous blood gas at the bedside immediately
12-lead ECG and continuous cardiac monitoring (hyperkalaemia/hypokalaemia risk with insulin)
Full septic screen for the trigger: temperature, chest/abdominal/urinary exam, cultures as indicated
Weigh patient (or estimate) for fluid and infusion calculations; insert urinary catheter if unwell for output monitoring
assessment: Diabetic ketoacidosis: BGL >11, capillary ketones ≥3 mmol/L (or urine ≥2+), venous pH <7.3 or bicarbonate <15 — confirm the diagnostic triad
Precipitant identified (missed insulin plus intercurrent illness) and consider euglycaemic DKA in anyone on an SGLT2 inhibitor even if glucose is near-normal
Assess severity and consider HHS, lactic acidosis and other causes of high-anion-gap metabolic acidosis as differentials
plan: FLUIDS FIRST: 0.9% sodium chloride IV — give a 500–1000 mL bolus (10 mL/kg) then continue per DKA protocol; fluids precede insulin
CHECK POTASSIUM before/with insulin: DO NOT start insulin if K+ <3.5 mmol/L until replaced; add potassium chloride 10–40 mmol/L to fluids once K+ <5.5 and patient passing urine
Fixed-rate IV insulin infusion 0.1 units/kg/hour (actrapid) started AFTER fluids are running — do NOT bolus insulin
CONTINUE the patient's usual long-acting basal insulin (glargine 18 units) alongside the infusion
Add 10% glucose IV (running concurrently) once BGL falls below ~14 mmol/L, and keep insulin running to clear ketones
Monitoring: hourly BGL and capillary ketones, venous gas and electrolytes 2–hourly initially, hourly obs, strict fluid balance, cardiac monitor
Treat the precipitant (e.g. antibiotics if infection confirmed) and give VTE prophylaxis; involve endocrinology/ICU per severity
Withhold any SGLT2 inhibitor; do not use bicarbonate routinely (only on senior advice if pH <7.0)

critical_errors: Starting insulin before fluid resuscitation, or starting insulin without checking potassium first — insulin drives K+ into cells and can precipitate fatal hypokalaemia; do not give insulin if K+ <3.5 mmol/L until replaced
Assuming a normal or near-normal glucose excludes DKA — SGLT2 inhibitors cause euglycaemic DKA; failing to check ketones and consider it
Stopping the insulin infusion (or omitting glucose) once BGL falls, leaving ketosis/acidosis uncleared
must_not_miss: Hypokalaemia identified and corrected before/with insulin
Precipitating cause (infection, missed insulin, infarct, pancreatitis) actively sought
